d: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene: a common, low-cost rigid plastic with a good surface finish, widely used for enclosures and consumer products.
The defect level used with a sampling standard such as ISO 2859-1 to decide whether a production batch passes inspection.
Polyoxymethylene: a stiff, low-friction engineering plastic used for gears, clips and mechanisms.
An injection-mould tool machined from aluminium: quicker and cheaper to make than steel, but it wears sooner, so it suits prototypes and lower volumes.
Spreading a one-off cost, such as tooling, across the units it helps produce, so it can be included in the unit cost.
An individual who invests their own money in an early-stage company, usually in exchange for shares.
Having different properties in different directions. A 3D-printed part, especially one printed by FDM, is often weaker between its layers than along them.
A process that grows a hard oxide layer out of the surface of a metal, usually aluminium. It can be clear or dyed, resists wear and corrosion, does not chip like paint and is electrically insulating.
The labour time needed to put a product together, which drives assembly cost on every unit.
Firing fine glass beads or similar media at a part to give an even matt texture that hides machining marks, often before anodising.

The stress in a part as it bends, highest at the surface furthest from the middle of the section and where the bending moment is largest, such as the root of a cantilever bracket. Compared with the material's yield or allowable stress, it shows whether the part will spring back or take a permanent bend.
The structured list of every part, material and quantity needed to make a product, used for costing, purchasing and assembly.

A connector that joins two circuit boards directly, stacked or at right angles, so they need no cable and locate each other. The housing must still hold both boards so the connector does not carry the load.

A programme run by some large online marketplaces that helps brand owners manage their listings and report copies. Such programmes generally require a trade mark, registered or applied for, in the relevant country.
Joining metal parts with a filler metal that melts at a lower temperature than the parts themselves. It distorts parts less than welding and can join different metals, but is permanent.
The sales volume at which total contribution covers fixed costs, so the product neither makes nor loses money.
Lower-cost, faster tooling used to make early production parts while demand and design settle, before committing to full production tooling.
Extra stock of a part or product held in reserve, so a late delivery or a sudden rise in demand does not stop production or sales.
How quickly a business spends its cash each month before it is profitable.
A structured argument that a product is worth developing, bringing together market, price, cost, investment and risk.
A fitting that clamps a seal around a cable where it passes through the wall of a housing, so water and dust cannot follow the cable in. It suits round cables of a known diameter.

The most common type of snap fit: a hook on the end of a short flexible beam that bends as the parts are pushed together and springs back behind a catch. The strain at the root of the beam must stay below the material's permissible strain.

A touch control with no moving parts that works through a solid wall, so it seals well and has nothing to wear. It needs light, sound or vibration as feedback, and gloves or water can stop it working reliably.

The greenhouse gas emissions linked to a product across the life cycle stages counted, usually expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent. It measures one impact, where a life cycle assessment looks at many.
The number of units packed in each outer case, often chosen to suit how a retailer orders. Changing it changes the case size and how cases fit on a pallet.
The movement of money into and out of a business over time. A profitable business can still run short of cash if money goes out before it comes in.
The lowest point of a business's cumulative cash forecast, which sets the minimum funding it needs.
The conformity marking used for many products sold in the EU and in Northern Ireland, and recognised in Great Britain for many product types.
A simple, recorded process for approving design changes once a design is frozen, because changes then affect tools, suppliers and test reports.
The share of the retail price kept by a retailer, distributor or marketplace.
A fit in which the shaft is always smaller than the hole, so there is always a gap. Used for parts that must slide, turn or assemble by hand.
Joining overlapping metal sheets by pressing them into an interlocking button, with no heat, fasteners or consumables. The joint is permanent.
Computer-controlled cutting of parts from solid material, used for prototypes, precise parts and low volumes.
Cost of goods sold: the direct cost of making and delivering each unit sold.
The visible colours, materials, textures and surface finishes chosen for a product, and how they look, feel and age. CMF is usually led by industrial design.
The classification number that sets the duty rate and import rules for a product.
Choosing between design concepts using structured criteria rather than preference.
A thin protective film applied over an assembled circuit board to help it resist moisture and condensation. It is lighter and less permanent than potting.
The process of showing a product meets the regulations that apply to it, by self-assessment or through an independent body.
Money set aside in a budget for problems that will happen but cannot yet be named; commonly 15 to 25 per cent in hardware development.
A company that sources parts, assembles, tests and packs a product to the customer's design.
Automatic protection for original works such as drawings, manuals, software and photographs.
Hollowing a thick feature of a moulded part so it is made of walls close to the nominal wall thickness. It avoids sink marks and voids, and shortens cooling time.
A face of a part that people will see or touch, marked on the drawing so that suppliers keep marks, defects and support or contact points off it and finish it to the agreed standard.
Lowering the cost of making a product that is already in production, for example by removing parts, operations or unneeded precision. Each change needs validating before it reaches production.
A footprint boundary covering raw materials and manufacturing, up to the product leaving the factory.
A footprint boundary covering a product's whole life: materials, manufacturing, distribution, use and end of life.
A dimension, function or property that decides whether a product works, is safe or is acceptable to the customer. CTQ features are marked on drawings and checked more closely than the rest.
Raising money from many people, often as pre-orders or rewards, before a product is made.
The average sales and marketing spend needed to win one new customer.
Talking to people who have a problem, about how they deal with it today, before designing a product to solve it.
The value on which import duty is calculated, usually the price paid plus transport and insurance to the UK border.
A one-off tool, often called a cutter, that cuts and creases sheets of card into the shape of a particular box. Changing the box shape usually means a new cutter.
The time taken to make one shot or one part on a machine, a key driver of part cost.
A feature, such as a face, edge, hole or axis, that a drawing declares as the reference from which measurements start. Datums are usually the features that locate the part in an assembly.
Delivered duty paid: an Incoterms rule under which the seller delivers to the buyer's premises with duty paid.
A signed statement by the manufacturer that a product meets the regulations that apply to it.

A name that simply describes a product or its qualities. Such names are generally hard to protect as trade marks, because other traders need to be free to use ordinary descriptive words; distinctive or invented names tend to be stronger.
Designing a product so it is quick and reliable to put together, for example with fewer parts and fasteners.
Designing parts so they can be made reliably and economically by the chosen process.
The point at which a design is fixed and further changes go through change control.

A short, structured meeting where the right people check a design against its requirements and risks, then decide whether it is ready to move to the next stage: proceed, proceed once named actions are closed, or rework.
In the UK, automatic protection against copying of the shape and configuration of a product.
Testing production-intent parts against the requirements before committing to production.
In Great Britain, a standard that gives a presumption of conformity with the relevant product regulations when it is met.
An off-the-shelf circuit board carrying a processor, radio or sensors with easy connections, used to prove electronics and firmware before a custom board is designed.
Forcing molten metal, often aluminium or zinc, into a steel die to make metal parts at volume.
Product information on materials, repair and recycling that the EU plans to require for some product groups under its ecodesign framework.
Selling directly to end customers, usually through your own website, without a retailer.
The slight taper on faces parallel to the tool opening that lets a moulded part release cleanly.
Requirements for the environmental performance of products, such as energy-related products, over their life.
The point from which a change applies, given as a date, a production batch or a serial number. Recording it means you can always tell which units contain the old part and which contain the new one.
A pin in an injection-mould tool that pushes the finished part out; it leaves a small mark.

A material's stiffness, written E and given in MPa on its datasheet; also called Young's modulus. With the second moment of area it sets how far a part bends, and for plastics under a load that stays on, the long-term (creep) modulus applies.
The ability of electrical equipment to work without causing or suffering unacceptable electromagnetic interference.
The greenhouse gas emissions from making a product's materials and parts, before it is used.

A plate or cap that closes an open end of an extruded enclosure and carries its connectors, lights and seal, usually screwed into the screw ports with a gasket against the cut end. Machined aluminium end plates suit low volumes; moulded plastic caps need a mould, so they usually come later.
The bill of materials for the product as designed. It usually mirrors the assembly structure in the CAD model and is owned by the design team.

A short, numbered record of a proposed change to a released part: what should change, why, and which part numbers are affected. It then carries the impact check, the approval decision and the effectivity, so the whole history of the change is in one place.
A prototype that integrates form and function to check the design against its specification.
A UK scheme offering tax reliefs to investors in qualifying smaller companies.
Designing a product to fit the people who use it: grip, reach, weight, balance, forces and comfort across the range of intended users.
A way of ranking market evidence from weak (opinions) to strong (payments and commitments).
Engineering, design and production validation testing: the last three development stages, as named in many electronics teams.
Rules that make producers responsible for the cost of managing their products or packaging at end of life.
A process that pushes material through a shaped die to make long parts with a constant cross-section, cut to length.

The steel disc, with the profile's shape cut through it, that heated aluminium is pushed through to make an extrusion. It is relatively simple, so it usually costs much less than a die-casting die or injection mould for a similar part, though cost rises with profile size, complexity and the number of hollows.
Ex works: an Incoterms rule under which the buyer takes responsibility for the goods from the seller's premises.
An O-ring seal in which the ring sits in a groove in a flat face and is squeezed as the two faces are pulled together, usually by screws. It depends on the faces closing fully and evenly.
The way in which a product or part fails, such as cracking, wearing, leaking or not switching on. Recording failures by mode makes patterns and their causes easier to spot.
An injection-mould tool that makes several different parts in one cycle.
Fused deposition modelling: 3D printing by extruding melted plastic filament layer by layer.
Putting a small batch of products into real use to learn how they perform over time.
A spreadsheet that links unit cost, price, volume, fixed costs and payment timing to show profit, break-even and how much funding a business needs.
Computer simulation of stresses, deflections or heat in a design, used to check it before building.

An order that commits the buyer to pay, as distinct from a forecast, which only helps the supplier plan. A supply agreement can say when orders become firm and whether the buyer pays for materials bought against a forecast.
The software built into a product's electronics that controls how the hardware behaves.
A detailed check of the first production parts against the drawings to confirm the process is right.

A thin, flat, flexible circuit that links boards at different angles or on moving parts, and is the same in every unit. It needs a defined bend shape with no sharp creases, and care at assembly because its connectors are small and easy to fit at an angle.
Free on board: an Incoterms rule under which the seller pays to load the goods onto the ship at the origin port.
Materials and parts intended to touch food or drink, such as containers, utensils and appliance parts. They need grades and evidence suited to that use, so check the rules early.

The usual test of whether a changed part is interchangeable with the old one. If it can still replace the old part everywhere it is used without any other change, it gets a new revision; if not, it gets a new part number.

A gasket made by dispensing a bead of liquid onto a flange by machine, which cures into a soft seal on the part. It follows complex shapes, but needs dispensing equipment and a groove or stop to set the compression.
Whether a product can be made and sold without infringing other people's patents or rights.
Storing, picking, packing and delivering orders to customers, done yourself or by a third party such as a marketplace.
The basis a footprint or LCA compares on, such as one year of use, so products with different lifetimes compare fairly.

Corrosion that happens when two different metals touch and are bridged by water, particularly salt water: the less noble metal, such as aluminium or zinc, corrodes faster. Using one metal throughout, or insulating the joint and keeping water out, prevents it.
A soft rubber or foam seal squeezed between two parts so it fills the small gaps between them. It needs a stiff flange and even, controlled compression to seal reliably.
The tolerance that applies to every dimension on a drawing that has none of its own, usually stated in the title block or by reference to a standard such as ISO 2768.

A system of drawing symbols that controls the shape, orientation and location of features, such as the flatness of a face or the position of a hole, measured from datums. It complements plus-or-minus size tolerances.
An approved reference unit that production parts are compared against.
A fitting in a hole through a wall that protects a cable from the edge of the hole. Where the product must be sealed, a cable gland or a sealed connector keeps water out.
Revenue minus the cost of goods sold, often expressed as a percentage of revenue.
The organisation that runs the barcode numbering system retailers commonly use. A business obtains its GTINs through membership of GS1 in its own country; in the UK that is GS1 UK.
Global Trade Item Number: the number behind a retail barcode, identifying one specific product to tills and stock systems. Each variant a shopper could buy needs its own.
A triangular rib that supports a boss or wall in a moulded part.
A tab with a hole or slot at the top of a retail pack so it can hang from a peg or hook in a shop. It must be strong enough for handling and let the pack hang straight.
An injection-mould tool made from hardened steel for long life and high volumes.
Fine surface cracks that form on a die-casting die as every shot heats it sharply and it cools again. They show as raised lines on castings until the die is repaired.
Finned metal, usually aluminium, fixed to a hot component to give it more surface area to lose heat. It needs moving air around it, so it suits vented products better than small sealed ones.

A threaded metal insert, usually brass, pressed into a hole in a plastic part with a heated tip, so the melted plastic flows into its knurls and holds it. It gives a thread that survives repeated assembly.

A hollow profile fully encloses at least one space, like a tube, so its die needs a mandrel supported on bridges; a solid profile, like a flat bar, encloses none. A semi-hollow profile nearly encloses a space through a narrow gap, like a C-shaped screw port, and can be harder to make than it looks because the thin tongue of die steel forming the gap is weak.
A heated channel system in a mould that keeps plastic molten up to the cavity, reducing waste and sometimes cycle time.
VAT charged on imported goods, normally reclaimable by VAT-registered businesses.
A treatment that seals the porosity in a casting so it cannot leak. For die-cast parts that must seal, ask the die caster about it alongside leak testing.
Placing a printed film in an injection-mould tool so it is moulded into the part, giving graphics that do not wear off.
Designing a product so it can be used by people with a wide range of abilities, ages and circumstances. Designing for the edges of the user group often makes a product easier for everyone.
International rules, published by the International Chamber of Commerce, that define who pays for transport, insurance and duty in a sale.

A bill of materials laid out in levels, with parts grouped under their sub-assemblies and quantities given per parent. It shows what a change touches, and a flat list of total quantities can be produced from it.
Making plastic parts by injecting molten plastic into a machined metal tool, cooling it and ejecting the part.
An optional level of packaging that groups a few unit packs together inside an outer case, to make handling and counting easier.
The UK's innovation agency, which runs competitions for innovation funding.
Creations such as inventions, designs, brands and original written or drawn work that the law can protect, through patents, design rights, trade marks and copyright.
A fit in which the shaft is always larger than the hole, so the parts must be pressed or shrunk together. Used where parts must stay put without fasteners, such as bearings and dowels.
Northern Ireland's economic development agency, which supports innovation and business growth.

Ingress protection rating: a code, such as IP54 or IP67, summarising how well an enclosure keeps out solids and water in standard tests. The first digit covers solid objects and dust, the second water; an X means that aspect was not tested.
An international standard for general tolerances, often quoted on drawings for dimensions that have no individual tolerance.
An area of a circuit board or enclosure where components, tracks or metal must not go, for example under a mounting boss or around an antenna.
A measure chosen to track progress towards a business goal, such as gross margin, sales growth or runway.
Overlapping walls that force water to take a winding path into a housing, keeping out splashes and rain without a seal. It does not wear out, but will not stop water under pressure or immersion.
The total cost of getting a product from the supplier to your warehouse ready to sell.
The visible ridges left on a 3D-printed part where each layer was built on the one below. They affect the look and feel of the part and, in FDM, where it is weakest.
The sloping face of a snap-fit hook that rides over the catch as the parts are pushed together, also called the assembly angle. A shallower slope makes assembly easier but needs a longer hook.
A standard method for assessing a product's environmental impacts across its whole life.
The gross profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship, including repeat purchases, consumables and accessories.
A moving part in an injection-mould tool that releases an internal undercut as the part is ejected.
A clear plastic part that carries light from an LED on a circuit board to the outside of an enclosure.

A part kept to show the worst acceptable version of a cosmetic feature, such as the largest acceptable gate mark. Production parts are compared with it, so cosmetic decisions do not depend on memory or opinion.
A thin, flexible section of plastic that acts as a hinge, typically moulded in polypropylene.
A model that shows a product's size, shape and appearance, but may not work.
The bill of materials for the product as built, grouped by how the factory assembles it. It adds things CAD does not show, such as glue, grease, protective film and packing materials.
Profit as a share of cost: (price minus cost) divided by cost.
Covering areas of a part, such as threads, fits and earthing points, so a coating, plating or anodising does not reach them. Masked areas should be few, simple and shown on the drawing.
A concentrated mix of pigment or additive in a carrier plastic, blended with natural plastic at the moulding machine to colour or modify the part.
A requirement that a grant recipient contributes part of the project cost from its own funds.
A document from a material supplier confirming the grade, batch and key properties of the material supplied. It helps trace and check what went into a part.

A flat switch panel bonded to the face of a product, usually under a printed overlay that carries the graphics on its back face. It seals the face in one piece and needs little tooling; metal domes can add a click.
A small patch of microporous membrane on a sealed housing that lets air through but blocks liquid water, so the pressure changes as the housing heats and cools do not strain the seal.
The smallest order a supplier will accept.
Multi Jet Fusion: 3D printing that fuses fine plastic powder, usually nylon, layer by layer, giving tough functional parts without support structures.
The machined metal tool that shapes parts in injection moulding or casting.
Simulation of how plastic fills a mould, used to predict problems such as short shots, weld lines and warping.
A matt or patterned surface made by texturing the surface of the mould tool, so every part comes out with it. Textured faces usually need more draft than plain ones.
A company that runs injection-moulding machines to make parts from a mould tool. It may also make the tool, or work with a separate toolmaker.
A mould tool that makes several identical parts per cycle, lowering cost per part at higher tool cost.
Non-disclosure agreement: a contract that keeps shared information confidential.
The price after VAT, discounts and channel deductions: what the business actually receives.
The standard wall thickness a moulded part is designed around.
Polyamide: a strong, tough engineering plastic that absorbs moisture, often glass-filled for stiffness.

A moulded rubber ring that sits in a groove and seals when squeezed between two parts. Because the groove controls the squeeze, it is one of the most dependable seals, and standard sizes are widely available.
Original design manufacturer: a company that designs and makes products, often adapting an existing design for a client.
Original equipment manufacturer: a company whose products or parts are sold under another brand or built into another product.
The shipping carton that holds a number of retail packs, usually with its own label and sometimes its own barcode. Retail stock usually moves in outer cases on pallets.
Moulding one material, often a soft TPE, over another part to add grip, seals or colour.
Printing that transfers ink from an etched plate to a part with a soft silicone pad, so logos and markings can be applied to curved or recessed surfaces.
Combining two or more parts that never move relative to each other into one, removing a part, a joint and an assembly step. The new part may need a new or modified tool.
The number of separate parts in a product. Each one adds tooling or set-up, stock, handling and assembly time, so reducing it is a core aim of design for assembly.
The line where the two halves of a mould meet; it can leave a visible mark on the part.

A chemical treatment for stainless steel that removes surface contamination, such as iron from tools, so the steel's own corrosion resistance works as intended. It barely changes the look of the part.
A registered right that protects how a new invention works, for a limited time, in return for public disclosure.
The time taken for cumulative returns to repay an investment.
The agreed timing and conditions of payment between buyer and seller, such as a deposit with the order and the balance before shipment, or payment a set number of days after invoice.
A blend of polycarbonate and ABS that balances toughness, heat resistance and surface finish.

The most strain a plastic can take in a flexing feature, such as a snap fit, without cracking or staying bent, taken from the material supplier's design data for the exact grade. Suppliers often give a lower figure for a joint opened many times than for one assembled once.
A small production run on the real process to prove it can make the product repeatably.

The record of which wire runs from which pin to which at each connector, usually given as a table on the harness drawing. Every harness should be checked for continuity and correct pin-out in production.
Depositing a thin layer of metal, such as zinc, nickel or chrome, onto a part for corrosion protection, wear resistance or a decorative metal look.

A Japanese term for error-proofing: arranging the design, fixture or process so a mistake cannot be made, or is caught straight away. Asymmetric parts that only fit one way and keyed connectors are common examples.
A very tough, heat-resistant plastic available in transparent grades.
A light, tough, chemical-resistant plastic often used for containers and living hinges.

Small pores inside a casting, from trapped gas and from shrinkage where thick sections freeze last; every die casting has some. Machining can open pores into a leak path on a sealing face or weak engagement in a thread, so machined features are kept in even sections.
Filling the space around electronics with resin that sets solid. It protects well against water and vibration, but adds weight and makes the board unrepairable.
A finish in which a dry powder is sprayed onto a metal part and baked into a tough, even coat. It comes in many colours and textures, builds up thicker than paint and is electrically insulating.

A ready-made radio module that has already been tested as a module. It reduces the radio testing a product needs, but it does not certify the whole product and its antenna guidance must still be followed.
Informal testing during development to find compliance problems before formal certification tests.
An order and payment taken before a product is available, used to fund and test demand.
A check of a sample from a finished, packed batch before it leaves the factory, against an agreed standard and sampling plan.
A quantity at which a supplier's unit price steps down. Asking every supplier for the same price breaks makes their quotes comparable.
The board that holds and connects a product's electronic components through copper tracks. Once the components are fitted it is often called a PCB assembly (PCBA).
The legal responsibility of producers for harm caused by defective products.
A written list of what a product must do, for whom, with measurable targets and constraints.
An early build that tests whether a product's core idea works.
A concept-selection method that scores options against a reference design, criterion by criterion.
An agreed description of inspections, acceptance criteria and responsibilities for making a product.
How long a supplier's quoted price holds, and the conditions, such as changes in material prices, under which it may be revised.
UK Corporation Tax relief on qualifying research and development spending.

An O-ring seal in which the ring sits around a plug or spigot and is squeezed against the wall of a bore as one part slides into the other. The fit sets the squeeze, which suits round lids and end caps.
The period after a successful pilot run when production builds up from first batches to full volume, while any remaining actions are closed.
A registered right protecting the appearance of a product.

A trade mark registered for particular goods and services in a particular country or region. The ® symbol indicates a registered mark and should only be used once it is registered, and only where it is registered; ™ can be used with a name you treat as a trade mark whether or not it is registered.
A request to suppliers for a price, sent with drawings, quantities and requirements.
Recommended retail price: the price the end customer is expected to pay, usually including VAT in the UK.
The face of a snap-fit hook that holds the parts together once assembled. At or near 90° to the pull the joint cannot be pulled apart; a shallower angle lets the hook slide out under a firm pull.

A recorded version of a part, drawing or bill of materials, usually marked with a letter such as Rev B. Each change raises the revision, so everyone can tell exactly which version they are working from.
Rules and expectations that products can be repaired, for example through spare parts and repair information being available.
A documented review of the hazards a product could present and how they are controlled.
Rules restricting certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment.
Working back from a reported symptom to the underlying reason it happened, so the fix removes the cause rather than the symptom. A common method is to keep asking why, sometimes called the five whys.

A statistical way of combining tolerances in a stack-up that assumes each varies randomly and independently. It predicts the range most assemblies will fall in, which is narrower than a worst-case analysis.

A turning control that counts steps, often with detents you can feel, whereas a potentiometer gives a position. Its shaft needs a seal, and it should be held in the housing so side loads stay off the board.
How a product reaches customers: direct, marketplaces, retailers, distributors or business sales.
Rules that decide where goods come from for trade purposes, which can affect duty under trade agreements.
How long a business can operate before its cash runs out at the current burn rate.

The allowable stress divided by the calculated stress: how much margin a part has. It is only as good as the allowable figure used; with the yield strength, a factor of 1 means the part is just starting to bend permanently.
A trade arrangement where a retailer can return unsold stock to the supplier, which keeps the stock risk.
The share of parts or products rejected during manufacture.
Printing that pushes ink through a fine mesh stencil onto a part, suited to flat or gently curved faces and larger areas of colour.

A channel built into an extruded profile, usually in the corners, that screws go straight into, so end caps can be fixed with no drilling or inserts. Agree its shape and size with the extruder and fastener supplier.

A property of a cross-section's shape and size, written I, that sets how well it resists bending; the material's elastic modulus sets the rest. For a flat bar it rises with the cube of the thickness, so doubling the thickness makes it eight times stiffer.
An alternative supplier or interchangeable part that can replace a component if the first becomes unavailable, so one shortage does not stop production.
A UK scheme offering tax reliefs to investors in very early-stage qualifying companies.
A nut, stud or standoff pressed into a hole in sheet metal so that the metal flows into its grooves and locks it in place, giving a strong thread in sheet too thin to tap.
A little controlled slack left in a cable so a board can be lifted out and unplugged without straining it. It should be clipped so it cannot wander into a seam.
A small discount offered to a buyer for paying an invoice early.
Parts made by cutting, punching and bending flat metal sheet, such as enclosures and brackets.
Outer cases designed to open into a display tray, so staff can put the whole case on the shelf without unpacking each unit.
A moulding defect in which the plastic does not fill the tool, leaving the part incomplete, often at the end furthest from the gate or at thin features.
A moving part of a mould tool that forms an undercut and slides out before the part is ejected.

A moulded silicone rubber part carrying one or more buttons, with carbon pills underneath that press on contact pads on the circuit board. Clamped round its edge it is both button and seal, with a softer press than a tactile switch, but it needs its own mould.
Soft moulds made from silicone around a master pattern, used for vacuum casting short runs.
A shallow depression on a moulded surface caused by a thick section shrinking as it cools.
Stereolithography: 3D printing that cures liquid resin with light, giving fine detail and smooth surfaces.
Selective laser sintering: 3D printing that fuses nylon powder with a laser, producing strong functional parts.
Fixing a part with a hole onto a plastic post by melting the tip of the post into a head, like a rivet, with a heated tool or ultrasonic vibration. Removing the part means cutting off the heads.

Describes a mould feature first cut so that any likely correction only means removing steel, which is much easier than adding it back. A hole might be cut slightly small so it can be opened up after measuring.
A neutral 3D CAD file format that most CAD systems can open, commonly used to share part models with suppliers.
A common file format for 3D printing that describes a part's surface as a mesh of small triangles. It loses the exact geometry, so a STEP file is usually sent as well.
A feature that takes the pull on a cable at the housing, so the force does not reach the connector or solder joints.

A feature that concentrates stress, such as a sharp internal corner, the root of a boss or rib, a hole near an edge or a sudden change in wall thickness. Cracks tend to start there, so generous radii help.

A written agreement setting the rules for a whole relationship with a manufacturer: specification and quality, tooling, IP, pricing, orders, delivery, payment, changes, responsibility for faults and how the relationship ends. Each purchase order then only deals with quantities, dates and prices.
The texture and appearance of a part's surface, such as as-machined, polished, textured, bead-blasted or painted. Finer or specified finishes usually add cost.
Cleaning and treating a surface before bonding, painting or coating, for example by removing grease and mould release, abrading or priming, so the adhesive or coating holds.

The first samples from a new mould sent to the customer to check against the drawing, before the tool is modified. Labels vary: many toolmakers call the very first shots T0, so agree what each label means.

A small switch on the circuit board that gives a crisp click after a short travel, usually pressed by a plastic button in the housing. It is made to be pressed straight down, so the button needs an end stop and the board needs support under it.
The most a product can cost to make and land while still meeting the business's margin at its price and route to market.
Taking apart a competitor's product to understand its parts, materials, manufacturing methods and likely cost.
The documentation that supports a product's conformity: design, risk assessment, standards and test reports.
A purpose-made rig that holds a part or circuit board in a repeatable position for testing or programming, often touching test points with spring-loaded pins.
A pad or contact on a circuit board placed so that a fixture or probe can reach power, programming or key signals during testing and production.
A soft, heat-conducting pad that fills the gap between a warm component and a heatsink or case wall, giving the heat a path out.

How strongly a heat path resists the flow of heat, in degrees Celsius per watt (°C/W): how many degrees warmer one end gets for each watt flowing through it. Resistances in a chain add, and the temperature rise is the power multiplied by the total.
Heating plastic sheet and forming it over a mould, used for trays, covers and large thin parts.
A usability testing method in which participants say what they are looking for, expecting and noticing as they work through tasks, so observers can see why they hesitate or make mistakes.
A screw designed to form its own thread in a plain hole in a plastic part, with no insert or tapping. The thread wears each time it is removed, so it suits joints opened occasionally.
The box of information in the corner of an engineering drawing, giving details such as the part name and number, revision, material, scale and general tolerance.
The total range a dimension may vary within, from its lower limit to its upper limit. How the bands of two mating parts sit relative to each other decides the fit.
The combined effect of tolerances on several parts on a fit or gap in an assembly.

Moving a production tool, such as a mould, out of a supplier's factory to the owner or another supplier. Agreeing in advance how it can be collected, how much notice is needed and whether any costs apply, such as packing or outstanding invoices, keeps that route open.
Who owns a production tool such as a mould, and so whether it can be moved to another supplier. It should be agreed in writing, with who pays for repairs and changes.
The company or specialist that designs and makes mould tools, and reviews part designs for mouldability before the tool is cut.
Thermoplastic elastomer: a rubber-like plastic that can be moulded and over-moulded.

A sign, such as a product or brand name or a logo, that tells customers whose product they are buying. It protects the brand, not the product's design or how it works; registration generally makes the rights clearer and easier to enforce.
Repeatable drop, vibration and compression tests that check packaging protects a product in shipping.
A fit in which the hole and shaft tolerances overlap, so some pairs have a small gap and some a slight press. Used for accurate location where parts still need to come apart.
A press tool that removes the runner, overflows and flash from die castings at volume. It is a separate cost from the die, so check it is in the quote.
The official GOV.UK tool for finding commodity codes, duty rates and import rules.
The conformity marking used for many products placed on the market in Great Britain.
A marking used alongside CE marking for some products in Northern Ireland.
Joining two plastic parts by pressing them together and vibrating them at high frequency until the interface melts and fuses. The joint is quick, strong and can seal, but cannot be undone.
A feature that stops a moulded part being pulled straight out of the tool.
The revenue, costs and profit attached to selling a single unit, used to show whether each sale makes money before overheads.
The pack a shopper sees and buys, holding one product and carrying its own barcode. It is the smallest level of retail packaging.
Watching representative users try to do realistic tasks with a prototype or product, without help, to find where they hesitate, make mistakes or work around the design.
Casting polyurethane resin into silicone moulds under vacuum to make small batches of production-like parts.
A structured review of what each part, feature and process step does for the customer, looking for ways to deliver the same function at lower cost.
Equity investment from funds in companies with potential for rapid, large-scale growth.
Checking that a product meets its specified requirements, through tests, inspection and analysis.
Distortion of a moulded part as it cools unevenly.

A promise that a product, or a supplier's work, will meet an agreed standard for a stated time, with what happens if it does not, such as repair or replacement. A brand may give one to its customers, and a supplier may give one to the brand on the parts it makes.
Waste electrical and electronic equipment: the regulations that make producers responsible for electrical products at end of life.
A visible line where two flow fronts of plastic meet in a mould.
The price a retailer or distributor pays the brand for a product.

A made-up set of wires cut to length with connectors, terminals and any sleeving fitted, built by the supplier to a harness drawing. Each harness gets its own part number and revision on the bill of materials.
Illustrated, step-by-step instructions for each assembly or test station, written so an operator new to the product can build it correctly at normal speed.
Cash tied up between paying for stock and being paid for it.
A model that proves a product functions, without needing to look like the final design.
A tolerance stack-up method that adds tolerances directly, assuming every part is at its limit at once. It is safe but can demand very tight tolerances.
The share of parts or products that pass inspection first time.
